children: Asian stocks slid on Monday November 23, as investors seemed to brace themselves for more market volatility after Wall Street's artificial intelligence (AI) led selloff.

South Korea's Kospi fell 3.74%, while Taiwan's Taiex dropped 0.93%. Hang Seng futures lost 0.9%. Japanese markets, meanwhile, stayed shut for the day's trade on account of the country's Labour Thanksgiving Day.
Chip heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI rally, opened in the red. The Kospi had started the session down 2.6% before the losses deepened.

Back home, the GIFT Nifty pointed to a positive, gap-up start for Indian equities. The Nifty closed near 25,800 last Friday after four straight weekly gains, and 26,000 now looks within reach. If profit booking sets in, the markets would be likely to look for support at 25,500–25,600.
China, Taiwan and South Korea announce market support measures

Regulators across Asia moved to calm nerves. China will cut the minimum margin requirement for leveraged share purchases to 80% from 100% on November 30. Xinhua, citing the regulator, said the step could free up $60 billion.
Taiwan widened its curbs on short selling and said it has been buying shares after the Taiex suffered its worst weekly drop in 35 years.

South Korean officials announced a stock stabilisation fund after an emergency meeting on Sunday. Analysts quoted by Bloomberg said that the government is preparing a 10 trillion won fund, though they called the size too small to lift near-term sentiment.
In major regional currencies, the Japanese yen weakened 0.3% to 159.01 per dollar, and the offshore yuan barely moved at 6.6738.
US futures rebound after Wall Street's worst weekly rout since 2020

US equity futures bounced as trading resumed on Sunday evening. S&P 500 contracts gained 1.9% and Nasdaq 100 contracts climbed 2.6%. Dow futures rose between 650 and 700 points. US Treasury futures fell as demand for haven assets cooled, while spot gold rallied 1.1% to about $3,575 an ounce after five straight daily losses.

Wall Street had ended Friday's trade deep in the red mark as the S&P 500 entered a technical correction and closed below its 200-day moving average. The Nasdaq 100 slipped into bear market territory at its intraday low and posted its worst week since March 2020. The VIX, which can be referred to as the Wall Street's fear gauge, jumped to its highest level since April 2025.

Several factors fuelled the rout, according to a Bloomberg report which includes, investors booking profits ahead of the Anthropic IPO, worries over Nvidia, key, and fears that the US Federal Reserve would hike rates aggressively. The MSCI Asia Pacific gauge now sits about 18% below its June peak, close to bear market territory.
Oil prices slip as traders weigh supply against West Asia risks
Oil prices meanwhile, fell as traders weighed signs of ample crude exports against the risk of wider fighting in West Asia.

Brent crude dipped below $92 a barrel to trade at $91.72 in early Asian hours, after closing 0.6% higher on Friday. US West Texas Intermediate hovered near $83, with the January contract down 0.7% at $82.86.

title: Kospi slumps nearly 4%; Asian markets fall as Wall Street sell-off deepens
